summary: The University of Illinois reply to a UCLA request for information on network graphics. It describes graphics support for application groups, including imitating the CALCOMP plotter package, producing output for the Network Graphics Protocol, and grey-scale work on several devices. It is an informal status report.

subtitle: Illinois' response on early graphics capabilities at the university.

today: RFC 472 is a historical record of early network graphics efforts at a major ARPANET university in 1973. The graphics technologies described are long obsolete.

sections.title: Graphics Support at Illinois
sections.content:
In March 1973, the University of Illinois responded to a UCLA request for information about network graphics capabilities. The response documents their approach to supporting beam-oriented graphics by closely emulating the CALCOMP plotter support package, a widely-used plotting system, but with output in the Network Graphics Protocol format.

This informal status report shows how one major ARPANET site was tackling the problem of making graphics work across networked machines, with local computing resources kept to a minimum and most computation done remotely at other sites.
sections.eli5: A university explained how it let scientists at the school send drawing commands over the network to a computer that would make a picture.

sections.title: Graphics Technologies in Use
sections.content:
Illinois' graphics work focused on several technologies. For most applications, they emulated the CALCOMP package with output to the Network Graphics Protocol (NGP). Some peripherals like the Gould 4800 required conversion to device-specific formats, though this was expected to be handled locally with the arrival of the ANTS MARK II and PDP-11/45 systems.

In addition to beam-oriented graphics, Illinois was performing grey-scale work on GOULD and IMLAC devices. One group processed satellite pictures, another produced natural-resource maps, and a third was generating holograms. Grey-scale standardization had not yet been planned.
sections.eli5: They had several drawing computers: one that made beam pictures (like an oscilloscope display), and others that made grey pictures (like photographs). Different machines needed different instructions.

sections.title: Interactive Graphics Vision
sections.content:
Illinois was planning an interactive graphics system that would use multiple hosts, possibly including a remote Evans & Sutherland machine for 3D operations like rotation and scaling. The prototype system demonstrated simple manipulation of meteorological data such as contouring and 3D plotting, with an IMLAC passively displaying the NGP pictures created.

The planned implementation included commands for MOVE, DRAW, TEXT, and UNDO operations with mouse and keyset input. Illinois recognized that different philosophies existed for distributed interactive graphics: one where all nodes understand a common command set, or another distinguishing between intelligent displays and computers. They favored the more general approach.
sections.eli5: They were building a system where scientists could use a mouse to draw pictures on a screen, with commands like 'move,' 'draw,' and 'undo' similar to modern drawing programs.

sections.title: Network Graphics and Standardization
sections.content:
Because Illinois had minimal local computing power for applications work, all graphics computation was done remotely at UCSD, USC-ISI, and UCLA-CCN. The distributed nature of their work meant they had much to gain from standards and were willing to cooperate with standardization efforts.

Their approach emphasized letting efficiency dictate the format of intermediate results shipped over the network, with standardization applied where it helped minimize effort. This pragmatic approach reflected the early state of network graphics in 1973.
sections.eli5: Most of the actual calculations happened at distant universities, so they wanted everyone to agree on how to send pictures over the network.
